utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I believe we are supposed to have some housekeeping, some responses from the Defence, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise. I didn't have my headphones on and I just now realised that you had already addressed us. I apologise. As regards yesterday's issue of the disclosure of the ex parte segment of our motion related to the witness, I have checked the situation, Your Honours, and it is completely in conformity with the Rules. The Defence is not under the obligation according to the Rules to actually submit to the Prosecution the address of the witness, and that is the only part which is ex parte, which is in full compliance with the Rules and we shall stick to that position. That is one thing. As regards this second question which is the issue of deadlines and the content of statements according to Rule 95 ter, overnight we studied in detail all the Rules which govern this subject matter and we have submitted a submission in that connection to you today which will be received by the Chamber today, so that we do not feel that we should actually discuss it in oral form in order not to waste time during this trial. The Defence has prepared copies of this submission for the Trial Chamber, for the colleagues from the Prosecution, and these are two motions, two submissions which refer both to the ex parte obligation of disclosure of particulars in relation to the witness, as well as to the 82(F) issue. Can I ask the usher to please distribute these copies to the Trial Chamber and to the colleagues from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that we understand one another, you have referred to two Rules which I'm not aware of. You referred to 95 ter and 82(F). It doesn't look like there is a 95 ter in the Rules, it doesn't look like there is a -- -- just give me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was inadvertently that I said 95 ter. I meant 92 ter, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 92 ter, as you will understand from the new Rule is dependent on 92 bis and 92 bis requires you, in subparagraph B thereof that the statement of the witness must be -- the declaration must be witnessed by a person authorised to witness such a declaration in accordance with the law and procedure of the state or a presiding officer appointed by the registrar of the Tribunal for that purpose. And B or 2, that the person witness in the declaration verifies in writing all those things. That the person making the statement is the person identified in the said statement, that the person making the statement stated that the contents of the written statement are to the best of his personal knowledge and believe true and correct. So and if you read -- that's 92 bis. Now, if you look at 92 -- what was I -- 92 ter in its new form, it says, the Trial Chamber shall decide after hearing the parties whether to require the witness to appear for cross-examination, if it does so decide, the provisions of Rule 92 ter shall apply. Now, this is C, paragraph C of 92 bis, okay. The provisions of 92 ter shall apply. And 92 ter then says a Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part that evidence, and this statement in terms of 92 ter comes from 92 bis. And 92 bis prescribes those formalities that I've mentioned to you. And it can only be so because now the 92 ter statement is now going to talk not only about general things but it also talks about the acts and conduct of the accused as charged. So it can only be under oath. I don't know whether you -- am I misunderstanding the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may I might be able to a -- if I may address this just briefly. Your Honour, I'm not sure about Your Honour's reading of the provisions. I'm not sure. I haven't looked at it quite that way. It's the first time I've thought about it that way, that is the inter-relationship between 92 bis and 92 ter and I have to give that some thought. I had rather read it otherwise which is that the formal requirements of 92 bis do not apply in the case of 92 ter because the witness comes into court and is under oath and says -- starts off his testimony saying this written statement is what I would testify to. So that in a sense takes care of the formal requirements which are contained in 92 bis. That's how I had read it but I had not considered Your Honour's reading and would have to take sometime. I see that the Defence has filed a written motion or response on this issue. I think it's sufficiently complicated that it perhaps might be worth us taking sometime to consider what they have filed, us meaning the Prosecution, and perhaps not take more time orally on it. I think it can be dispensed with that way. With respect to the ex parte issue though I would like to address that briefly if I may. There, I think with respect, I think Defence has counsel misunderstood the issue. The issue is not, as Defence counsel has stated both orally and also in the written submission that he just provided to us, it is not whether the Defence has an obligation to provide the Prosecution with certain particulars of witnesses. I agree they do not have that obligation. That's not the issue, however. The issue is that they -- is when they can provide something to the Trial Chamber without providing it to the Prosecution. The Rule, as I understand it, is that when we provide things to the Trial Chamber, they must be provided to the opposite party unless, there is a good reason for it to be provided ex parte. The Defence has not provided a good reason why we should not be given that ex parte filing. And it is their burden to demonstrate why, if they give it to the Trial Chamber, why we cannot have it. Having failed to do that, having been given an opportunity and having failed to do that, they should be ordered to give it to us, as a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There you go, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I wanted to ask Mr. Milovancevic a question because my understanding is that the decision to make the annex ex parte and not to disclose and deliver to the OTP was based on precedent as a result of practice. I believe that learned counsel had referred to an authority, but my addressing the rules it does not seem as if there is a Rule that would give the authority for this. What is your authority, Mr. Milovancevic? Is it something in the rules or is it just a question of practice?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we draw both on the rules and jurisprudence. The colleague Prosecutor failed to submit to us precisely this -- these data which are in the ex parte submission, that is to say the address, the telephones and other particulars for a whole series of witnesses. So all we are doing is endeavouring to ensure such conditions as will induce the witnesses to indeed agree to come and appear in this Court, and I believe that that is in the basic interest of this case and of this Chamber. The witnesses feel jeopardised for definite reasons, so they are asking us when their safe conduct is in question, that their addresses are not submitted to the colleagues from the Prosecution because this is what the witnesses do not want. On the other hand, Your Honours, we have had some bad examples as regards the attitude of the Prosecution's investigators towards our witnesses because in our impression, some sort of pressure was exerted on our witnesses, they were asked to give subsequent statements to the Prosecution, without us having been contacted previously. And even through the police, this was sought to be elicited, which is out of the ordinary. Now, we have overcome that question. I'm not raising this in order to broach a new issue. I'm just trying to explain why we did what we did. So we had exactly the same material submitted to the Trial Chamber and to the colleagues in the Prosecution. The only thing which they do not have which is ex parte is this particular, which we do not wish to disclose and deliver for the reasons I've just explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What about the Rule? Up to now in your explanation, you haven't provided me with the Rule which to me would be material. All that you have said, I'm waiting to hear which is the relevant Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is no provision in the Rules which directly governs this subject matter, but there is a provision in 89(F) which regulates the question of work with witnesses and it says, I believe it is 89(B), I can check, it says that in dealing with witnesses, the practice which is in keeping with the interests of justice will be applied and which is in keeping with the spirit of the rules of the Tribunal. Rules and statute of the Tribunal. If it is in our interest, and it is, for the witnesses to appear, and if some particulars about witnesses from the practice of the Prosecution, have been withheld from the Defence, we fail to see why such practice, and this particular provision of that particular Rule, should not be interpreted in a way which would be conducive to the coming of witnesses to appear before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: 89(F)? Or (B) rather says [Microphone not activated] Rules of evidence which best favour a fair determination of the matter before it, and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law. It says in cases not otherwise provided for in this section a Chamber shall apply rules of evidence, et cetera. So that is what that is dealing with. But I believe Judge Moloto wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do indeed have something to ask. First of all Mr. Milovancevic, I just want to ask you one or two points. You say that the Prosecutor or the Prosecution approached some of your witnesses without your prior knowledge and what have you. Was this after they -- the Prosecution had known that those are your witnesses or were they still just people at large and they were looking for witnesses? At what stage were they approached?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether the colleagues from the Prosecution knew that the mentioned people were witnesses at the time they approached them, but in the concrete instance, the witnesses told them that they had already given us a statement but despite that, they continued to exert pressure on them to come and be witnesses for the Prosecution. It is only upon that happening that the Defence intervened by telling our colleagues that the Prosecution had already submitted a list of their witnesses and had prepared their detailed and final versions of briefs, and that in such a situation, such a request directed at our witnesses was illegitimate. Of course, later they actually dropped that demand in respect of two specific witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I can't take that point much further until and unless we hear further from the opposite side. Let me ask you the next question or let me raise the next issue. You say that there is no rule and you're looking at jurisprudence and that the Prosecution also did not give you particulars of some of their witnesses. Now, I don't know or I don't remember the circumstances and I'm not suggesting you're not -- they didn't do so. They may very well have done so. If I understand Mr. Whiting's argument, in such a case where particulars are not given, reasons are given in the motion why those particulars are not given. So that the party who does not receive the particulars can see in the motion why he's not receiving the particulars. And as I understand his argument, he's saying, in this case, the Defence has not done so, has not given reasons why they should not be obliged to disclose the particulars of the particular witness, and in that event, then he argues that normal practice should take place. I should just say that you can't say because the Prosecution did it we are also doing it, without following the proper procedures, and if it is indeed so that where the particulars are not disclosed, and are given ex parte, that reasons are given for that, then you should be able to give those reasons before you -- together with the filing, not from the bar as you are standing there and saying, oh, no the reason we are doing is this because the Prosecution has approached our witnesses, the reason we are doing this is because they have done it before. Mention those in the motion. Now, it may very well be that you have mentioned those reasons in the motion. I don't have any recollection of the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is exactly what I was about to say, Your Honours. Before today's submission of our learned colleague from the Prosecution, we submitted to you now a written submission about that particular situation, even before our colleague from the Prosecution actually complained about the situation, we submitted this written submission to the Trial Chamber precisely on that account and for that reason. That is the first of the two submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you're not absolutely correct there, Mr. Milovancevic. This issue was raised yesterday and you filed this filing today. So you are filing it after they have raised the issue. Yesterday, we postponed this issue because you were going to investigate it, after they had raised it. You cannot now say today's filing was filed before they raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please take into account one thing: This is maybe our 14th or 15th witness. We haven't had any such complaints so far. Why does this appear as a contentious issue? Because such practice prevailed during the whole trial. Yes, you are right that we submitted something in writing before the submission of the opposite side in the form that they expressed it today. We did not perceive this as a problem, this issue. This is the only thing that I'd like to say. We had no intention of breaching the rules or establishing a new practice. We -- the Prosecution hasn't reacted to such practice so far in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, I have not kept track of every motion that you ever filed, I don't know whether this is the first time you are filing a motion without disclosing these particulars or whether you've done it before and the Prosecution has not objected. The question of the matter is that they are now objecting at this stage and when you now say you have made -- you have filed a filing before they've raised issue, you are not correct. That's all I'm -- I'm responding to you. You are not correct because the issue was raised yesterday. Now, instead of addressing that, you jump into the next one and say this is the 14th witness, you have been doing it all the time. I can't really be running after every little reason that you give because your previous answer has not now been sustained. I think you got to give your reasons once and for all and we argue those reasons all at a time, not give reasons when the one fails, you know. I don't know why the Prosecution, if indeed they have been accepting these filings without particulars being given, I don't know why they are objecting today. They probably have a good reason. They are here to tell us. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, on that issue I'm not sure if it's a good reason or not, I just noticed it with this filing. It may have occurred in previous filings and we didn't object to it not -- it wasn't something I was focused on. It's not something I think that if we don't object in an earlier case we waive it. I do accept that perhaps Defence counsel thought that it had become the practice and that he could do it without giving reasons. I understand that. That's fine. However he's now being asked to give reasons and I don't think -- I have not from our point of view -- we have not heard a reason yet why we cannot have the ex parte filing. Now, while I'm on my feet, if I may just address a few other points that were raised, in particular, I would like to address the suggestion or even allegation that we have contacted witnesses and pressured witnesses and so forth. I can state categorically that this team, the Martic Prosecution team, has not made contact with a single Defence witness since we obtained a list of Defence witnesses. That -- unless it happened without me knowing about it which would surprise me quite a bit. I'm -- I am certain that that has not happened. I am aware that one witness, one listed Defence witness, was somebody who had agreed to be a Prosecution witness in another case which is being prepared for trial, trial is to start shortly in that other case. That witness was contacted because he had agreed to be a Prosecution witness, he had given a statement to the OTP, signed statement, and he indicated when he was contacted by that other team that he had -- was now a Defence witness in this case. And I believe that was the end of the matter. He was dropped from that other case. I'm not aware of any pressure that was put on him or anything of that sort. But in any event we have not gone out to contact the Defence witnesses. I will say, however, that there is nothing in the Rules or the jurisprudence that prevents us from doing so. We have every right to go and contact Defence witnesses on our own without contacting the Defence. There is no obligation that -- for us to tell the Defence that we are doing that or to do it through the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not part of the practice of the Tribunal, you're saying, that when it's known to a party that a witness is the -- a person rather is the witness of the other party, there is no Rule of practice even that requires that he not contact that person?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is no consistent rule of practice, Your Honour. There have been practices adopted with respect to particular trials and in some cases, the parties have often times -- what happens is the parties themselves come to an agreement about how they are going to do that, what procedures they are going to follow to contact the other party's witnesses. But as far as I know, there is no consistent practice, no Rule, no jurisprudence, which required -- which would require us, as the Prosecution, to go to the Defence, to tell them that we are contacting their witnesses or to get their permission or to do it through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could the Defence equally during the course of this trial make contact with the Prosecution witness and not make disclosure to the OTP? Because I would find that highly irregular. I must tell you that I am struggling with that thought violently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is something -- and I understand and I understand Your Honour's reaction and this is something where practice in different national jurisdictions differs quite a lot. And therefore, people who come to the Tribunal come with their own practices and try to -- and tend to try to implement those. For example in my country, there is no -- nothing which prevents the parties from contacting other witnesses and doing so without telling the other party. And I'm aware that practice is radically different in other countries. In any event, if I may say, the point is academic for us because it's not something we have done. And if we had contemplated doing it, I don't know whether I would have told Mr. Milovancevic or not. I never had to reach that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must say -- okay, finish. I'm itching to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. But in any event, I reject and in fact resent the sort of off-the-cuff oral suggestion that we have somehow acted improperly with respect to the Defence witnesses that we have pressured them and that this is now a justification for this ex parte filing. Those allegations are simply false. With respect to the Rules and a basis for doing this, I do think that Rule 69 is perhaps a basis for withholding information under certain circumstances with respect to witnesses and it has to do with protection of victims and witnesses. And it all -- and this gets into the area of protective measures and protecting the security of witnesses. And the Prosecution, it is true, will at times rely on this Rule to withhold certain particulars about witnesses or delay the disclosure of witnesses to the Defence. However, I don't think that this is a case where the two sides, it's not a parallel, it's not parallel. What we do when we disclose things to the Defence, it is not comparable to when the Defence is disclosing things to us. So I don't think the Defence can rely on things that we have done in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The difference, Your Honour, is that when we disclose information, we are disclosing it to the Defence and we are disclosing it to the accused and that's the difference. When the Defence -- there is no accused war criminal sitting on this side of the courtroom and I don't mean that with any disrespect. It's just whether you're talking about witness security measures that is a relevant difference and it is the basis for why we at times are able to delay disclosure or withhold certain particulars, such as personal details of a witness, address, because it's being disclosed not just to the Defence but also to the accused, and that may raise security considerations with respect to the witnesses. I cannot imagine what security situation arises why the witnesses are endangered in any way if the information is disclosed to us. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milovancevic, I have a few clarification issues to raise with you. If you can just give me a chance, if you don't mind. I said I'm itching to talk and I said so simply because I just found that statement that you made completely incomprehensible and completely unacceptable in my judicial culture and I could not, and if you say it's academic, I say it is not academic. It is an issue that needs to be decided and decided very clearly in this Tribunal so that the matter is put to rest once and for all. If you say that there are different practices in various Trial Chambers, that is not good enough for me and I think it's something that needs to be decided once and for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear. With respect to this issue, I'm happy to agree that if we -- if our team makes contact, wants to make contact with any Defence witnesses, I'll let Mr. Milovancevic know. I'm happy to agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. That doesn't stop me from just emphasising exactly my feeling about it. It is so important an issue for me that if it is transgressed, I cannot see how it can be said there is fairness in the trial. So, for me, it's a very strong issue. And I'm grateful that in fact you are prepared to talk to Mr. Milovancevic about it if it should happen. I take your point that you say it has not happened. I take your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand completely Your Honour's reaction. I have to say though from my culture I see it completely the other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And even find it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've heard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And even find it a difficulty and a problem that the parties would -- that parties have a sort of control and a guard over their own witnesses and that they sort of possess them. So there is a cultural difference, but I fully appreciate Your Honour's point of view on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, and let me for instance, let me at least say and you'll remember that I asked Mr. Milovancevic whether according to his information, did the -- whether the Prosecution approached his witnesses after the Prosecution had known that those were Defence witnesses. Now, it's a complete no-no for me if the Prosecution does know. It is something else if you stumble across a witness and you discover while you're talking to the witness that he's offered himself to the other side and I would imagine that courtesy would require that one withdraws at that point. However, the reason for that, for saying to me it's a complete no-no is that there is a very high likelihood of information passing from the one side to the other inadvertently which may jeopardise the position of the other and I think it should not happen. That's why I say fairness would not come -- and once a list of witnesses has been given, I think it behooves the other side to respect that list and not approach those people. Accidental meetings are put aside. The other issue now we've kept so much long and this one that I've forgotten, the second issue, I wanted to raise with you. I hopes it comes back to me. Mr. Milovancevic, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There was just one question I wanted to pose to Mr. Whiting. Mr. Whiting, have there, in fact, been instances when there was a motion and ex parte annexes where the information was disclosed to the Trial Chamber and withheld from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. That certainly was done from the Prosecution with respect to protective measures motions. We had at least one protective measures motion where certain details and reasons why protective measures had to be granted were provided in ex parte annexes to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you may have provided this information to the Trial Chamber before, but in those instances, what was your authority? Practice merely or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. I would think it's -- it's certainly Rule 69 and any other Rules -- I believe there is also one other Rule which I can't put my fingers on at the moment which deals with witness security. But it would have to do with -- it would have to do with that with respect to witness security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, Rule 69, though, deals with applying to the Trial Chamber in order to do that. It doesn't seem to speak to the party having the right to adopt that course without the leave of the Trial Chamber. Am I having a wrong reading or could you direct me to the relevant portion that would specifically permit you to do that? Because I must admit that I don't see it the way that you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, no. Your Honour, I do not believe that there is any Rule, at least not one that I'm aware of, which specifically regulates when the parties and under what conditions the parties can file ex parte annexes to the Trial Chamber. I think that the thinking is that it's implicit in the Rule, with respect to witness security, that if we are seeking witness protection measures from the Trial Chamber, and in order to do that have to disclose certain things which if disclosed to the other party could jeopardise that witness, that we can apply to do that ex parte and we have done that ex parte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is it fair to make a distinction between the OTP and the Defence in relation to that Rule merely on the basis that on one side is OTP and that they have less of a propensity to commit acts to the prejudice of a fair trial or to the prejudice of the other party's case? What reason is there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the question I was going to ask. That reminds me of what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think I would have put it quite like that, that the -- that one side has less or more of a propensity to commit acts to prejudice a fair trial. I really don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I reformulate the question because that's the question I had forgotten? As I understood your argument, precisely because of the presence of the accused on the Defence side, it is felt that the Defence is more likely to jeopardise the security of the witness than the Prosecution would because there is no accused on the side of the Prosecution. That's what you said. Now my question is -- several of them or two of them. When confidential information is given to the opposite side and the opposite side is bound in terms of the Rules not to disclose this to anybody and keep it to themselves and to seek permission of the Chamber before they can disclose it and bind those parties - there is a Rule that says that - is the accused not part of this whole Defence team that must be bound by this? Number 1. And if the accused is not part of that, what is the point of delaying certain, such confidential information until within 30 days of hearing when such information is given, and what is -- what would stop the accused, if he comes to know that information within 30 days, from giving it away and endangering the security of that witness if he -- unlike if he got it earlier than 30 days early?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that what's at issue here is that there has to be a balancing between the interests of the Defence and the interests of the accused to have the information that is required in order to fairly defend their case and the reality that the accused is an accused who -- where there is a prima facie -- there is an indictment, there is a prima facie case of -- that the -- that supports that indictment, and while the accused may be bound, as a technical matter by the Rules of non-disclosure, it does not change the fact that the accused is an accused under indictment. And the -- I'm grateful that Your Honour has raised the example of the 30-day non-disclosure because that is exactly the -- that is exactly the sort of proof of this point. The reason that we are permitted to -- and we have been permitted by this Trial Chamber and by other Trial Chambers to delay disclosure of witness identity in certain sensitive cases until 30 days before that witness testifies is precisely because there is a risk, a risk that we have to demonstrate, that we have a burden to show and we have been able to show, that if it's disclosed earlier to the Defence, then the witness's security may be jeopardised. That has been our proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is simple, Mr. Whiting: What guarantees the security 30 days later?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no guarantee. But when it's 30 days before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it worth the paper it's written on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the name is out there for a year, as opposed to 30 days beforehand, I think that one can say that there is a greater danger if it's out there for a year. There is more opportunity for tampering and for witness -- and violating the witness's security. And 30 days beforehand, that is the point where the interests of the accused lies so that we have got to turn it over. The balancing tips the other way and we -- we cannot obviously keep it from the accused forever and so the balancing is struck at 30 days between those two interests. So I disagree with Your Honour that such measures are not worth the paper they are written on. They are not perfect. They are not guarantees but they are the best we can do and they show precisely the point I'm trying to make, which is the interests in these two different directions is not the same, and the Defence simply cannot get up and say, well, they with held information, therefore we can with hold information. That's not good enough. They have got to say why it is that there is a need to withhold this particular information from the Prosecution. And if the reason is well, the Prosecution is going to go tamper with our witnesses, I'd like to hear the basis for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two issues, very briefly. I share the opinion of Her Honour Nosworthy that access to the other party's witnesses at the moment when the statement was taken is against the Rules. Well, the Rules do not expressly prohibit that. It may be presumed that it could be allowed. But whoever leads a witness, they have the right for examination-in-chief. Then the other party may cross-examine. Then re-examination in joinder, then rebuttal, so Rules have to be construed within a certain logical system connected and to determine what a certain Rule means. By applying Rules we also interpret them, Your Honour. My opinion is if the OTP has reached a certain witness and reported that witness as theirs, I may work with that witness only during cross. Otherwise, the Rules would be breached. That's one point. The other point concerning disclosure of particulars to the other side. One of our witnesses, I cannot remember the code, he was a protected witness, that witness, at the moment when he was announced as a witness and immediately before coming to witness, experienced such nasty things in Banja Luka that police had to check their address, et cetera. He was a protected witness. Another witness who testified after that one experienced approaches from the OTP, and when Mr. Whiting, I accept when he says that it is a normal situation when the OTP does not have information about that person being our witness. That's one thing. But if they already know that somebody is our witness, then they are breaching the rules of common decency and I believe that the Rules force them to stand back and wait for their opportunity during the cross-examination, and this is how I see the matter. The question raised by the OTP when it comes to disclosure, we, as the Defence team, are in possession of a piece of information that we received from the accused, that Defence witnesses, when coming back home, were experiencing very bad, nasty things. They were mistreated, harassed, arrested. We are talking about small countries. Everybody knows everybody and people are afraid of such consequences. I want to say that the Defence team, by approaching the Chamber to obtain safe conduct wishes to create the conditions for witnesses to approach this Chamber and testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, let's not repeat ourselves, but let me just raise this issue again with you because you have repeated it. It is not good enough to tell us about the unfortunate experiences of some other witness that has testified or that was called by the Defence at some stage and use that as a reason for not disclosing the particulars of this one. That is why you got -- when you apply for protective measures or safe conduct you've got it tell us what is it in respect of this specific witness that makes you not disclose or that makes you want protective measures or that makes you want safe conduct. And if you are saying that your witnesses are being harassed, that may very well be so or that may not necessarily be so, but what are the facts in relation to this specific -- each case must be treated on its merits. That's the rule. Each case must be treated on its merits. Now, the thing is you haven't told us - perhaps you did now by today's filing but I haven't read that filing yet because I've been busy talking with you - you haven't told us what is it with respect to this specific witness that makes you want to file ex parte. I can't remember the other thing that -- well, on the question of the Prosecution having to respect your witnesses once they know, I share your view. Mr. Whiting doesn't share the view, but nonetheless, he has said if he does know he will make sure that he respects that. So there is no need for us to go back to that one. And I'm not sure by saying this specific witness had been approached by the Prosecution, and if he hasn't been approached by the Prosecution, what are the specific and peculiar circumstances of this witness that make it appropriate for you to seek an ex parte filing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for this concrete witness, we submitted to the Chamber and the OTP reasons why we sought safe conduct. The only remark of the OTP was that we did not disclose the address and telephone number, and since they broached this subject yesterday, we wrote today this filing responding and provided reasons why we did so. This is the only issue broached by the OTP. Everything else falls outside of the boundaries of what you just said. It covers a much wider area. Your Honour, if by your leave, I propose the following. The Chamber can always rule on this subsequently after the break or maybe tomorrow. Since the -- this witness has some other engagements in his schedule, he's supposed to be travelling back home tomorrow, and he should still be cross-examined, maybe we should be seized of this matter before the next witness comes to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then, that sounds like a very helpful suggestion. We have spent a lot of time discussing this point and we are not getting to any resolution. I think we will deal with it by way of a written decision. Does that bring us to the end of the housekeeping matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, thank you. And I apologise for taking so much time. I actually had not expected it would take so much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hadn't either. Shall we call the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I approach the accused for a moment for some consultations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Martic drew my attention to his outrage by the statement of the OTP that we on our side do not have a war criminal sitting here. We have to presume innocence and everybody is guilty until a final verdict is taken. I would like to ask from the Bench, or the Chamber, to remind the OTP to respect the dignity of the accused in this courtroom. Providing arguments on legal issues and points of law cannot be based on the besmirching of the accused's character.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's at page 13, line 18, and it says, accused war criminal. We do not have an accused war criminal sitting on this side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I think this language is a little imprecise, isn't it, from a logical point of view. Friction with the presumption of innocence is contained in such a language and I was also feeling uncomfortable with that I must confess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it was a bad choice of language but I, with respect, think it was absolutely clear. I've been a Prosecutor for 15 years. I know -- I'm very familiar with the presumption of innocence. I respect it and I'm certainly respecting it here in this courtroom today and I know that Mr. Martic is not convicted. He's an accused. And I've always referred to him as an accused and nothing more. And I apologise if my language was not more clear in that respect but I really think it was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That's often the case with misunderstandings, isn't it, that oneself thinks the language is not clear and one learns it's not clear or has not been clear. Therefore, your offer for an apology is very valuable I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just say that I'm trying to find it on the transcript but I'm not finding it, but I do clearly remember Mr. Whiting using words to the effect that we are -- we know that Mr. Martic has not been convicted but there is a prima facie case that has -- which is the basis of the indictment that is before court. But having said that, having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is then that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Having said that, particularly for people who speak different languages, I do think, Mr. Whiting, it may be a little unfortunate to use accused war criminal. It's something to say a person accused of war crimes, you know. The word "criminal", even though preceded by accused, may be interpreted by speakers of other languages to mean something different from what I think you wanted to mean. And I can hear what you say, but simply because we come from diverse cultures and diverse language backgrounds, I think it would be helpful if we use language that is absolutely clear, that we are sitting here with somebody who is accused of war crimes and therefore, A, B, C, D.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I take Your Honour's point and Judge Hoepfel's point very clearly and I just hope it's clear from the language that I used in various things I said that I did not intend anything more than to say that Mr. Martic is accused and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I referred to your referring to prima facie case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Having said that, I just want to say to Mr. Martic, on behalf of the Chamber, we just want to apologise to you for any unfortunate meaning that may have been conveyed to you by the statement. I hope you have heard Mr. Whiting's explanation. He never intended to suggest that you're a criminal. He just suggested that you happen to be accused of the crimes. Okay? And we appreciate you raising the point with the Chamber if you feel uncomfortable about it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess Mr. Black is supposed to be -- [Microphone not activated] it's your turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before it is your turn, can I just make my turn? Good afternoon, sir, I will not call you by name but I still do recognise you and recognise your name and when I say "witness", I don't mean disrespect. Just to remind you once again that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness is yours, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, hello. Good afternoon. I know you have plans and we are going to try to get you out of here so you can catch your flight tomorrow. So I am going to try to cover a lot of ground quickly. If you can help me out by focusing on my questions, please. The first issue -- and I believe we are in open session and we can remain in open session, yes. You testified a little bit about the structure of the RSK police and in particular, on Friday, at transcript page 65, you said that the special purpose units of the RSK police ceased to exist as of 29 November 1992. Do you remember telling the Trial Chamber about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were referring to the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But that wasn't true, was it, because the special police units continued to exist in 1993, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in that form. So no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, maybe in another form but essentially with the same name. In 1993 there were still special purpose police units, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were not. The special police units from 1992 until the date which you said existed in the form of a temporary formation, the basic function of which was to guard the border line which is within the ambit of the Ministry of the Interior and after that, no such units under that designation existed but there were smaller units within each SUP which were named special units. Their task being predominantly to intervene where there was a need or there was a fear that there might be the application of force or to counter infiltrated terrorist groups. So these were the units that existed at that time. They were quite different from the previous ones and they were very small in strength, the number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me be very specific about what I'm suggesting, and this is a reference to Exhibit 730 which I don't think it's necessary to pull up, but, sir, in 1993, the RSK police had essentially two departments, the regular police which consisted of approximately 7.000 men was supposed to deal with maintaining law and order and other traditional police business. The other department, to use that word, was the special purpose police which was intended to consist of about 16.000 men and their job was to police the RSK borders and to protect the population from terrorist attacks, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that you changed the year. I'm not aware of that. But certainly not. Definitely not. Perhaps you can assist me by telling me who was in charge of those units, the name or surname of a commander or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: According to Milan Martic in December of 1992, he was in charge of overall internal affairs and the department of special purpose police, I believe, was commanded over by a General Novakovic. Does that help refresh your recollection of this structure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you are wrong again. In 1992, the commander of the special police units was Mr. Djukic, and in 1992, on the 19th of November, those units were disbanded and the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established at the helm of which was General Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so if Milan Martic said in December of 1992 that the structure would continue to be as I have stated it, then he was either wrong or not stating it accurately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Martic stated. I know that you were wrong when you said what you said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well let's move on to another issue. I think we are clear on your position there. Members of the special purpose police for the most part were not professional policemen, right? They didn't have police education prior to joining the RSK police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority, most probably the majority, did not have that. I cannot say with precision but in view of the duties they had to perform in agreement with the civilian police, a certain number of people needed to be recruited. So they were not qualified as classical policemen but they did not police the standard rule and law and order but policed the border line. Let me remind you that in 1991, the president of Croatia, Mr. Mesic, distributed 54.000 badges of police members.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you answered the question. I don't want to get us off on to another topic. In fact, the special purpose police were more of a military formation than a police formation, right? And this follows a little bit from what you said about their activities and they didn't do traditional police activities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did not do traditional police activities, but performed duties within their legal powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And their duties are more accurately characterised as military than police, right? They carried long weapons and they knew very little about traditional police work; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many countries, the police guards the border, and ipso facto has that form of activity to perform as well. In view of the fact that there were war operations going on, what you have said is also quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, not asking you about many countries. I'm not asking you about normal, but is it correct what I have said, that they were essentially military rather than police, that they carried long weapons, that they didn't do traditional police work? Is that correct? Not is it normal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can only repeat what I've already said, they were police forces doing police work. If you believe that in your view that was more of military work, that means that you are changing actually the legal regulations prevalent in the area of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, sir, no, let me interrupt.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I do agree, from that particular aspect, that they could be seen as doing more of that kind of work but that was in keeping with the legal prescriptions and practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not really focused right now on this question about the legal prescriptions and practices, but so do I understand you correctly that you agree that they could be seen as doing more military work than police work? Are we in agreement on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say they discharged police work which involved more military competences than is the case with the traditional police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the United Nations at least considered the special purpose police units to be paramilitary units? That's the way the United Nations saw them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that position. I know that the civilian police, the UNPROFOR organs of the police, cooperated with those units in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, the United Nations considered the very existence of the special purpose police to be a violation of the Vance Plan, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you aware that according to the UN, the special purpose police engaged in ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You suggested on Friday, and I think this was at transcript page 67 of that day, that the RSK created the SVK because in its view the United Nations had failed to prevent violations of the Vance Plan by Croatia. That was -- that's your point of view, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But do you know that the point of view of the United Nations was that the existence of these special purpose police violated the demilitarisation provisions of the Vance Plan? That was the way the United Nations saw it, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm quite sure that you're wrong there. Let me remind you I'm quite sure that you know that, that the special police units were formed by the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which was a signatory of the Vance Plan and a guarantor for its implementation. The Republic of the Serbian Krajina was not a signatory of the plan. On the basis of the agreement concluded for the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army to withdraw from the area, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia wanted to solve that question in a territory which was still under its competence and that is why these special police forces were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, in fact, you say that they were established by the SFRY but the special purpose units in 1992 were really just a continuation of the special purpose units that existed in 1991, and in fact the structure continued into 1993, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no connection whatsoever. The first units were the other ones. This was a completely new structure arising from the Vance Plan, and based on the decision, I believe, I cannot be sure, of which body but it was a body definitely of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you dispute that the people who joined the special purpose units in 1991 continued to serve in those special purpose units in 1992 and 1993? Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand your question. I'm not clear on whether it was prohibited for individuals to go to one or another unit. I don't understand the question. There were some members who joined some of those units and then others joined other units but I don't know that. If I have managed to answer your question, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you have. My point is that there was continuity between the special purpose units in 1991 and in 1992 and into 1993 and one of the aspects of that continuity is that people who joined in 1991 would stay in those special purpose units all the way into 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've said clearly that there was no continuity and anyone who consults the legal regulations, the norms and the dates of establishment will ascertain that. I don't know how these 1993 units can have any connection with the previous ones. This was a completely new structure. There is no connection whatsoever between the two kinds of units at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity? Notwithstanding the change in the regulations and in the law, is it not so that the people who composed the special purpose units in 1991 continued to be in the special purpose unit in 1992 and 1993? In other words, as I understand the question from the Prosecutor, is -- there was a change in name and a change in the regulations, but on the ground there was no change. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm quite sure that this is not so. If we proceed from just one state of facts, which is that the special purpose units numbered 16.000 people, as the Prosecutor said, I don't know what that number was, and I don't know what their strength had been before that. They certainly had not existed in that strength and in that form. They were certainly under -- probably under 1.000 people strong and therefore, there is no connection between the two units. Now, whether someone from the previous units joined the other units, I have no idea. And if they did, it is a much smaller number than the units, the previous units had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which time period are you saying they were 1.000 people strong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I don't know their number, but I don't believe that before 1992 there had been a thousand of them. I cannot say with certainty. But I do know that this number referred to as their number from 1992 is something which cannot be so. As far as I remember, on Friday, I said, not all the units had been formed, eight brigades were supposed to be formed and I believe only four were established and the other ones were actually disbanded, were not established but that was not part of my job so I cannot talk about these matters in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. I'm sorry I disturbed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No problem. I have just have a couple more questions I'd like to do before the break. They are very short, I hope. And these again come from Exhibit 75 essentially. I don't know if I mentioned that for the use of the Defence and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, Milan Martic told UNPROFOR in 1992 that the Vance Plan was not acceptable in its present form and it needed to be amended. Is that correct? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know concretely about these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. My last question just before the break is: In part on the questions, the things that we have been talking about for the last 10 or 15 minutes, contrary to what you said on Friday and I believe again yesterday, the United Nations was hardly satisfied with the work of the RSK police, was it? In fact, they made constant complaints to the RSK police about specific incidents and about more work that needed to be done, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, two facedness was their constant and it's possible certain representatives of UNPROFOR who contacted us may have been two-faced as well. They may have told us one thing and written in their reports something else. Yesterday, you gave us a document where Mr. Thornberry discusses the quality of the cooperation between UNCIVPOL and our police, and he stated it was good and I wouldn't dare to negated what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, just so that's clear, that wasn't a document that I showed to you. That was a document that Defence counsel showed to you. And while you mention it, you weren't present at the meeting that was referred to in those minutes, were you? And consequently, you can't state one way or another about whether those minutes are accurate, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting, but I wasn't there when UNPROFOR drafted their reports, but what I can say is drawn from my own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You weren't at the meeting, consequently, you can't say yes or no if the minutes are accurate to that meeting, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that it was correct from the point of view of the person who kept those minutes, knowing his character.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But you weren't there and so you can't really say. That doesn't seem to be a controversial point. Do you agree with me that you weren't there and consequently you can't really say whether or not the minutes are accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that you agree that I cannot accept the minutes taken by UNPROFOR, then I would not accept the minutes taken -- you wouldn't accept minutes taken by our side but that -- this would lead us no where.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, answer the question. Don't go to another question or give speeches about UNPROFOR. It's not a difficult question and I think you need to answer it so that we can take our break. You cannot vouch for the accuracy of those minutes, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee or say that this -- these minutes are not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you -- and you can't say that they are correct, can you? It's not a difficult question, sir. Answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to ask my answer to be accepted. I stated three times clearly what I hold to be true about these minutes but the OTP cannot accept that this is an insinuation. I can vouch that it is correct to the same extent that I can say it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you don't choose the questions that you have to answer. The questions are chosen either by the Defence or by the person who asks the questions. I'm going to ask that we take a break and we can carry on with that question when we come back. Court adjourned and come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, you had a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, I'm really doing my best to get through there material quickly because we understand that you have other business to attend to and we also have a trial to get on with, but if you refuse to answer simple questions that slows everything down. So I'm going to ask you hopefully just one more time. You've said you weren't present at the meeting with regard to the minutes that we saw yesterday. And because you weren't there, you can't say that those minutes are accurate, nor can you say they were inaccurate. You just can't personally confirm or deny the accuracy of those minutes; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm the morality and the righteousness of the person who drew these minutes and to that extent, I hold these minutes to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you can't personally confirm or deny their accuracy, right? I didn't ask you about the morality of the person who took them. It's a simple thing. You weren't there and you can't personally say whether they are accurate or not, can you? I'm going to keep asking you this question until you answer it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. This sentence of the Prosecutor is connected to the previous ones, in terms if you do not answer in the manner that I want you to, then I'll keep badgering at you until you miss your plane tomorrow. Why should I trust this document and distrust another document? This is the matter at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You addressed yourself to Your Honours. Now I said to you before we went on the break that you don't chose the questions that you get asked. You've been asked a question and it's not a very difficult question. You can answer whether you can confirm that the minutes were accurate or you can't vouch for the accuracy. It's as simple as all that. And if you say that you have been badgered by the Prosecutor, then you are the author of that badgering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't intend going into an argument with you. Just answer the question put to you. Can you confirm the accuracy of the minutes or can't you? I don't think there is anything difficult or tricky about that. If you are not asked about other minutes, that is so, but you're being asked about these minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I confirm the accuracy of these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On what basis can you confirm the accuracy of the minutes that we are talking about now, if you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis -- on the same principle that I can confirm the accuracy of other meetings -- of minutes of the meetings that I did not attend and accuracy of documents that I had nothing to do with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So I guess you're saying that as you testify here, you're more than happy to talk about things that you don't even personally know about but you're willing to confirm or deny things based on suppositions or speculation. Is that the way I should understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. I believe that you are speculating and I am telling things as they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I guess I'll move on. I think I've beaten that horse as much as I can, Your Honours. Witness, yesterday we talked a little bit, and perhaps too abstractly about the issue of how many Serbs were victims of crime as opposed to Croats and things like that. So I want to put it in extremely concrete terms for you now. And to do that could we please see on the ELMO Exhibit 909. I apologise, on the e-court, talking in the old lingo. On the e-court, not on the ELMO. Sir, what you see before you is a report from the Knin SUP, in fact, dated 16th of August 1994. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we -- I think scroll down just a little bit on that first page, you'll see that it says there that 16 -- perfect -- 16 people were murdered in 1992, I take this to mean in the area under the jurisdiction of the Knin SUP, of whom five were Serbs and 11 were Croats. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read whether it's 11 or 16. I cannot see the figure. It's supposed to be 11 because 16 persons were killed, five Serbs and then it makes it a 11 when it comes to Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there on the original why it's difficult to read but I appreciate your answer. If you look at the list, and we will start with that third name there, Mate Slavic, it says that's a Croat and the perpetrator of that murder is unknown. Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll up to see the heading? Thank you. We can scroll back down to the text. Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course. That third name there, Mate Slavic, it says was a Croat and the perpetrator is not known, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in both the B/C/S and the English, you see -- so if we could look at the top half of that document, you see a name there, Marko Agic. Again a Croat, and according to this he was killed by a Croat. Then the next entry refers to three people with the surname of Bura who were Croats. The perpetrator of that crime is unknown according to this document. The next name, Vuza Slavic, another Croat, also unknown. Then the next one down, two Croats with the surname, Edsigovac, again the perpetrators are unknown. Sir, my question is that in 1992, according to this document, of all the 11 Croats who were murdered in this area, all of those crimes remained unsolved except for one where the perpetrator was a Croat, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was so. It is written so but I believe it wasn't so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you believe in the morality of the person who wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe, but I do not believe -- well, this document should contain some other things. This document was drafted in 1994. Am I right? And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you do believe the morality of the person who wrote it, why don't you believe the truthfulness of the document? That's the argument you used a little earlier about the letter -- about the minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I believed in the morality but I believe it was not complete in certain things. I wanted to finish my sentence. As far as I can see the date here, the date of the murder of these -- in the case of Bura is 7th of July 1992, and I don't know what happened previously. Maybe I'm wrong, but I'm being led to believe -- well, it is important where people were killed, whether in the villages that the demarcation line or line of separation went through because after the attacks of Croats on the Miljevac plateau --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. Just forget it. You may continue, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could I just ask a question before you continue. Beside Marko Agic, I don't know if that's the right pronunciation, in the fourth line, is it under offence where it says bad blood? What exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presumably, it refers to a personal conflict between the two persons, but I cannot really tell you what actually transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is that an offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we look down now just a little bit on the page, in B/C/S and in English, we get to the year of 1993. There it says that 13 people were murdered. And again I take this to refer to the jurisdiction of the Knin SUP because that's who drafted this document. Of those 12 murders -- there were 12 murders, 13 people murdered, one Slovene, three Croats and nine Serbs. That's what it says, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we scroll down just so we can see the rest of the page there. Actually, as it's being scrolled down, I can already point your attention. There were two Croats with the surname Palinic, perpetrator unknown, Josip Zelic, a Croat, in that case actually there are two perpetrators identified. Based on those names, I don't know if you're able to tell us, sir, whether the perpetrators were Serb or Croat. Perhaps you just don't know. Do you have any comment on those two names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which names did you mention? I was looking at somewhere else. I was reading the text, three Croats, nine Serbs, and in the four cases, the perpetrator remained unknown. Which names did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First, I just briefly referred you to the two Croats with the surname of Palinic where the perpetrator is unknown, and then further down, near the bottom of the page in B/C/S, you see the name Josip Zelic, another Croat, and there are two perpetrators named there and I don't -- I simply don't know if it's possible for you looking at those names to know whether those were Croat or Serb perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to tell whether they are Serbs or Croats. I presume that they may be Serbs judging by their first and family names but I would like to supplement what you said for the previous year 1992. This is why I thought about these data. At 1992, there was the murder of the Cengic family and I cannot find these names here. The perpetrators were Croats. They were apprehended and prosecuted. So I'm not clear as to who wrote -- drafted this document because, as I said, there were other things going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well thanks for that clarification and we will talk about the Cengic incident after we are done with this document maybe. And I understand your explanation that it's just -- it's not possible to say with certainty the ethnicity of those two people mentioned, although based on the names, you could guess they were Serb, but that's not definitive. So thank you for that. If we go to the next page in B/C/S -- thank you. There near the top, the third name is that of Luka Skoric, another Croat, and again the perpetrator isn't identified. Sir, my question is just that you've expressed that you think there may be information that's not included here, but based on this document, it would suggest that murders of Croats were solved by the police in Knin much less frequently than murders of Serbs. Isn't that right? In 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only appears to be so but that is not the fact because not all the data has been actually given, and I think -- I cannot remember their names of course. I believe that most of these murders took place in villages along the demarcation line where other forces had jurisdiction, not the civil police. The inspector of the police could only subsequently come to inspect the scene. This is of course not meant to justify any crimes but this was certainly the period after the Miljevacki plateau where several tens of Serbs were killed in atrocious ways and perhaps this was a case of revanchism, of retaliation, but only in that area. Of course, I'm not saying this in terms of any justification of any crimes. I just wanted to stress that the jurisdiction of the organs of the Interior in these border areas, because this was a special area under special control was only once an incident happened to have the organs come to the scene and inspect the scene, and therefore, perhaps they were that inefficient. There were no other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. We are done with that document for the time being at least. I'll ask you just about a couple of other specific incidents or time periods, I guess, not even necessarily particular incidents. For example, you testified on Friday that in 1992, the Croatian population in Benkovac was maltreated to some extent, is the way you put it, and that some Croats were killed there in Benkovac in January and February of 1993. Do you remember telling us about that topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about the instances of maltreatment and also that there had been some murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, in just one week, in February of 1993, somewhere between 11 and 17 Croats were murdered and one woman was raped in the Benkovac area. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the accuracy of the figures but it is quite certain that there were killings in that period, and we, as the organ of the Interior, certainly undertook the necessary measures. That is also true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I waited for the witness to respond to this question, and then I'm going to raise an objection of general nature. Either 11 or 17 persons were killed. It was either 12 or 13 or 14. If the Prosecutor presents to the witness as authoritative information that it was either 13 or 14 or 17 people that were killed, that lacks seriousness. And I'm pointing to this because we dealt with this question previously with another protected witness who actually pointed to that problem. So I should like to kindly ask my learned colleague to tell the witness exactly whether it was 11 or 17 people that had been killed and then we will get the right answer. And also, a woman was raped. If a woman was raped, what was her name? Let's hear her name and let us hear the names of these 11 or 17 victims because the Prosecutor is submitting very difficult facts to the witness which I'm not going to comment on any further for the witness's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you want the Court to do if you waited until the witness had answered because now the question has been asked and answered. In any case, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm almost at a loss. I don't see what's inappropriate about me putting a range of figures. I don't know how many people were killed in that particular time. I don't know this woman's name but I can still put a question to the witness which he was easily able to answer. And I would say that this comes straight from an exhibit in evidence, 729, just putting our case to the witness. He didn't seem to have any trouble with it and I also -- so I'm not sure what the basis for the objection is but I see no basis for not being able to answer that kind of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what ruling to give, Mr. Milovancevic, because the question has been answered and indeed I don't understand the basis for the objection myself. It's between 11 and 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to say that every and any victim is a terrible thing. If the colleague Prosecutor wants to ask the -- this specific question of the witness, let him ask him that very specifically, because we saw the names, the dates given in this document and the possible outcome of the proceedings, and whether there was the perpetrator had been detected or not. So I just wanted to draw the attention of the Prosecutor with all due respect to the fact that this -- raising this question in this way can hardly be relevant and serious. We have heard a lot of things about UNPROFOR reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milovancevic, now that you venture that as a basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Prosecutor doesn't have the name of a single victim and doesn't know anything about it, and he's actually just fishing and speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But your witness has answered the question, Mr. Milovancevic. I don't know what you want us to do. Are you still having questions on this point, Mr. Black? Or are you going to the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
